sermon:
There is a kind of letter you sit down to write with joy and finish with your jaw set. You meant to send congratulations and you ended up sending a warning. Jude knows that feeling. He tells us plainly that he was eager to write about one thing and had to write about another.

He opens like a man who loves the people he is about to alarm. "Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ" (Jude 1). Three words sit at the front of this letter before any threat is named: called, beloved, kept. He wants the church to know who they are before he tells them what they are facing. And his greeting is not a small wish. "May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you." Multiplied, not merely maintained. He is asking God to pour out more than these people have yet known, because they are going to need more than they have yet known.

**He wanted to write about salvation**

Then comes the turn. "Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints" (Jude 3). Hear the disappointment in it. He had a different letter in his heart. He wanted to write about the salvation they shared, the thing that bound them together, the good and settled center of their life in God. That is what a pastor wants to write about. The riches. The grace. The home we are going to.

Instead he found it necessary. That phrase is not the language of preference. It is the language of a man who has seen a fire and cannot keep walking. Something had happened in the church that made the warm letter impossible and the urgent letter required. I know that pull. I would rather preach comfort to you than danger. I would rather spend a Sunday on the mercy of God than on the men who twist it. But Jude teaches me that love does not always get to choose its subject. Sometimes love is forced to the harder word.

**Why he could not**

Verse four tells us why. "For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ." Crept in unnoticed. Not stormed the gates. Crept. They were already inside, already seated, already trusted, and no one had marked the door. And what did they do with grace once they were in? They turned it into permission. They took the most beautiful word in the Christian vocabulary and made it a license to sin. Grace became an excuse for the flesh, and the Lord who bought them was quietly denied.

This is the part I cannot preach from a safe distance. The men Jude warns about did not come in waving a flag that read heresy. They came in agreeing with us, smiling with us, using our words. The grace of God is real, and I have leaned on it, and I have also been tempted to lean on it the wrong way, to treat the mercy that cost the cross as though it cost nothing, to let it loosen me where it should have held me. The corruption Jude names begins as a small private bargain in the heart of a believer who likes grace better than holiness. We did this. I have done this.

So Jude tells the church to contend. To fight for the faith once for all delivered. Not a faith we invent and not a faith we update, but a deposit handed down, finished, entrusted to ordinary saints to guard. And the One we contend for is the same Master these men denied, Jesus Christ, who is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us blameless. The faith we defend is finally the faith He secures. We hold the line because He holds us.

Defend the faith you received.

We do not believe in judgment until we read history. Then the room goes quiet. Jude knows this, so he does not argue about whether God judges the ungodly. He reminds. He takes the church back through their own story and lets the record speak.

"Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe" (Jude 5). Stop on that. The same people He rescued, He later destroyed. Rescue from Egypt was not a guarantee of arrival in the land. A generation walked out of slavery and fell in the wilderness because they would not believe. Jude is telling a church that knows it is rescued: do not assume the exodus settles everything. Unbelief in the redeemed is not a small thing.

**A stack of warnings**

Then he piles on the examples, and the pile is the point. The angels who did not stay where they belonged, who left their proper dwelling, God has kept in chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day. Sodom and Gomorrah, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire. Israel. Angels. Cities. Across heaven and earth and time, the verdict is the same. No category is exempt. Power did not protect the angels. Privilege did not protect Israel. Prosperity did not protect Sodom. Jude is building a wall of precedent so that no one in the church can say it could never come here.

And notice the strange comfort buried in the warning. These judgments are not chaos. They are settled. The angels are kept. Sodom serves as an example. God is not improvising His justice. It is on the books. Which means the false teachers who crept into the church are not getting away with anything, however confident they look on a Sunday morning.

**Named by their fruit**

From there Jude turns to the men themselves and describes them with a precision that should make every preacher nervous. They defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme. They follow the way of Cain, run into the error of Balaam for profit, perish in the rebellion of Korah. He calls them hidden reefs at the love feasts, shepherds feeding only themselves, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, wandering stars. Then the verdict on their mouths: "These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage" (Jude 16).

Read that last line slowly, because it is not a list of monsters. It is a list of ordinary sins wearing a religious coat. Grumbling. Discontent. Doing what I want and calling it freedom. Flattering the people who can do something for me. I have grumbled. I have flattered. I have followed my own desire and dressed it as conviction. The terror of Jude 16 is how familiar it sounds. The false teacher and the faithful man do not always look different from the outside. They look different in what they are feeding and where it ends.

That is why Jude exposes fruit. Present sin is not waiting for a future verdict. It already sits under a settled one. The grumbling at the love feast is the same root that fell in the wilderness, the same root God has judged before and will judge again. Sin in the church is not a phase. It is a precedent repeating itself.

And here is the only ground to stand on when the wall of precedent has done its work and you feel your own name in it. The God who judged the ungodly is the same God who, through Jesus Christ, is able to keep us from stumbling and present us blameless. The examples are real, and so is the keeping. We do not survive the verdict by being better than Israel. We survive it because He holds what we cannot.

God has judged the ungodly before.

When a letter has spent most of its length naming a threat, the ending tells you what the writer actually believes will save you. Jude spends nineteen verses on danger. Then he tells the church what to do, and finally he tells them who will finish it. The order matters.

First he reminds them this is not a surprise. "But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, 'In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions'" (Jude 17 to 18). The scoffers are not evidence that the faith failed. They are evidence the apostles told the truth. The church is not living in a collapse no one foresaw. It is living in the very season it was warned about. That is steadying. The mockers at the edge of the room were on the schedule.

**What the church is told to do**

Then four commands, plain and active. "But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life" (Jude 20 to 21). Build. Pray. Keep. Wait. This is the ordinary labor of a believer who intends to last. Build yourselves up, not on novelty but on the most holy faith you were handed. Pray in the Spirit, because contending is not finally won by argument. Keep yourselves in the love of God, which means stay in the place where that love is felt and obeyed. Wait for mercy, because the end of this is not our verdict but His.

And notice he does not stop at self-defense. "Have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh" (Jude 22 to 23). A church under threat is tempted to harden into a fortress and let the waverers drown. Jude will not allow it. Go after the doubting. Snatch the slipping ones out of the fire. Show mercy even while you hate the sin clinging to them like a soiled garment. The same letter that says contend says have mercy. The fight for the faith is not a fight against the fragile. It is a fight to keep them.

**Then he turns**

Here is where the letter breaks open. After all the commands, after build and pray and keep and rescue, Jude turns from our effort to God's power, and the relief of it is almost physical. "Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen" (Jude 24 to 25).

Keep yourselves, he said in verse 21. He is able to keep you, he says in verse 24. Both are true, and the second is the ground of the first. We are told to keep ourselves precisely because we are kept. I have spent years trying to hold a grip strong enough to be sure of heaven, and Jude takes the weight off my hands without taking the work off my back. The work is real. The grip that finally holds is His. He is able to keep you from stumbling. Not from ever wobbling, but from the fall that does not get up. And He is able to present you blameless, which is the most outrageous word in the letter, that men and women like us could be set before the glory of God without a stain, and not in fear but with great joy.

This is the Christ connection the whole book was building toward. Not the God who merely warns, but the God who keeps, through Jesus Christ our Lord. The faith we are told to defend is finally held by the One who defends us. Contend with everything you have, and then rest, because the keeping was never yours.

He is able to keep you.
